title: The 90-day plain-English AI plan
subtitle: A humane learning plan built around short sessions, small artifacts, and real life.
intro: This plan assumes you have a job, a family, or a questionable relationship with your calendar. Three focused sessions a week are enough. Every week has a small finish line, every phase has a checkpoint, and two flex days are built into each 30-day stretch. You do not need to finish every resource—the plan is the spine, and the library is the shelf you choose from.
timeNote: Standard pace is about 4–5 hours per week. On a hard week, do the first task only. On a good week, add the stretch. Progress is not a personality test.

phases.title: See clearly
phases.summary: Get the vocabulary, practice a real prompt, and build a habit of checking the output. The goal is calm competence, not speed.

weeks.title: Make a small, safe start
weeks.focus: Orient, choose one safe problem, and put learning on the calendar.

tasks.label: Take Google's 45-minute Introduction to Generative AI.
tasks.detail: Finish the quiz if you want the free skill badge. Save two examples that feel genuinely useful.

tasks.label: Create one learning note with a no-sensitive-data rule.
tasks.detail: Name it something plain, like ai-lab.md. Add three tasks AI might help with, then circle one that uses no patient, client, financial, or password data.

tasks.label: Block three 45-minute sessions this week.
tasks.detail: Calendar them. Put your notes in one place. A small repeatable slot beats a heroic weekend.

weeks.stretch: Skim the five learning paths and choose a home base.
weeks.outcome: One safe starter task, one place for notes, and three appointments with yourself.

weeks.title: Learn the words
weeks.focus: Replace vague AI anxiety with a handful of accurate, plain-English definitions.

tasks.label: Work through the first two chapters of Elements of AI.
tasks.detail: No math needed. Write down one thing AI cannot do well.

tasks.label: Build a six-term glossary in your own words.
tasks.detail: Define model, prompt, token, context window, hallucination, and inference. If a definition needs a second jargon word, simplify it.

tasks.label: Explain one concept back in five sentences.
tasks.detail: Write it or record a voice note. Notice where you reach for jargon and where the idea is genuinely yours.

weeks.stretch: Watch one 3Blue1Brown neural-network video and sketch the idea afterward.
weeks.outcome: A one-page glossary you can actually use in conversation.

weeks.title: Practice the prompt loop
weeks.focus: Move from 'please make this better' to instructions you can test and improve.

tasks.label: Take the free lessons in ChatGPT Prompt Engineering for Developers.
tasks.detail: If you do not code yet, watch for the patterns rather than copying the API details.

tasks.label: Write a five-part prompt template: task, context, constraints, format, and example.
tasks.detail: Test it on one real, non-sensitive task such as rewriting a public paragraph or planning a meal from ingredients you already have.

tasks.label: Change one variable at a time and compare two outputs.
tasks.detail: Log which version was more useful and why. This is how prompting becomes a skill rather than a stack of magic phrases.

weeks.stretch: Read Google's prompt-engineering whitepaper for the reasoning behind the template.
weeks.outcome: A reusable prompt template and notes on why it works.

weeks.title: Make a tiny useful thing
weeks.focus: Turn the vocabulary and prompt practice into one edited artifact and your own safety rules.

tasks.label: Make one small artifact with AI help: a checklist, email draft, study guide, or scene.
tasks.detail: Use AI for a draft. Do the final editing, fact-checking, and decisions yourself.

tasks.label: Fact-check every factual claim and add a 'how I checked' note.
tasks.detail: Prefer primary sources. If you cannot verify something, label it as uncertain or remove it.

tasks.label: Complete Kaggle's Intro to AI Ethics and write five personal AI rules.
tasks.detail: Cover privacy, verification, disclosure, human review, and one situation where you will not use AI at all.

weeks.stretch: Show the artifact to one trusted person and ask what felt confusing.
weeks.outcome: A finished small artifact, a verification habit, and a personal rules card.

milestone.title: Day 30 checkpoint: you can explain it
milestone.description: You do not need a credential yet. You need evidence that the ideas are becoming yours.
checks: Explain generative AI to a friend in five minutes without hiding behind jargon.
Show one artifact that you edited and checked yourself.
Name three types of information you will never paste into a consumer AI tool.
Choose one next step: stay on this route or move into Python and data.

phases.title: Build the mechanics
phases.summary: Add Python and data skills, train a first model, and practice honest evaluation. Keep the artifacts small enough to finish.

weeks.title: Python, gently
weeks.focus: Learn enough code to read, run, and modify a small script—not to memorize a language.

tasks.label: Complete Kaggle's Python course.
tasks.detail: Type every exercise. Do not copy-paste your way through the first pass.

tasks.label: Write a 20-line Python script with a variable, list, loop, and function.
tasks.detail: Use your own text file or simple numbers. No personal data yet.

tasks.label: Start a bug log: error, guess, what fixed it.
tasks.detail: Three lines per bug. It becomes evidence of progress when the results feel invisible.

weeks.stretch: Try the first project in freeCodeCamp's Scientific Computing with Python curriculum.
weeks.outcome: Enough Python to be curious rather than afraid.

weeks.title: Make data legible
weeks.focus: Learn to inspect tabular data before you try to model it.

tasks.label: Complete Kaggle's Pandas course.
tasks.detail: Focus on selecting, filtering, grouping, and missing values.

tasks.label: Load a public dataset, check its shape and missing values, and make two charts.
tasks.detail: Use Kaggle datasets or a public open-data portal. No private business data yet.

tasks.label: Write a five-sentence data story and one thing the data does not show.
tasks.detail: The second part matters as much as the first. A chart without a limitation is a sales pitch, not analysis.

weeks.stretch: Clean one messy column and document every choice you made.
weeks.outcome: A notebook and a habit of asking what the data cannot tell you.

weeks.title: Train a first model
weeks.focus: Build the simplest model you can and learn why the score is not the whole story.

tasks.label: Complete Kaggle's Intro to Machine Learning.
tasks.detail: Train a decision tree and a random forest. Note the difference in results.

tasks.label: Work through the ML framing, regression, classification, and overfitting sections of Google's crash course.
tasks.detail: You do not need every module. Prioritize the ones that explain evaluation.

tasks.label: Explain train, validation, and test sets using a non-tech analogy.
tasks.detail: If the analogy breaks, fix the analogy, not your honesty.

weeks.stretch: Read the early chapters of Machine Learning Yearning.
weeks.outcome: A first model and an explanation of why a single score is not proof.

weeks.title: Tell an honest story
weeks.focus: Turn a dataset into a small project with a clear question, baseline, and limitation.

tasks.label: Choose a public dataset, one question, a baseline, and a train/test split.
tasks.detail: Write these down before modeling. A baseline can be as simple as predicting the average.

tasks.label: Train a simple model and record two metrics—not only accuracy.
tasks.detail: Explain why each metric fits or fails the question.

tasks.label: Write a README with the question, data, method, limits, and next step. Ask one person for feedback.
tasks.detail: This is the portfolio piece you can show later. Clarity beats complexity.

weeks.stretch: Try Kaggle's Intermediate Machine Learning for pipelines and cross-validation.
weeks.outcome: Project 01: a small, honest data story with a README.

milestone.title: Day 60 checkpoint: you can build and evaluate
milestone.description: You have moved from talking about AI to making a small, testable artifact with data.
checks: Run a Python script from top to bottom without step-by-step hand-holding.
Show one notebook with a question, two charts, and a stated limitation.
Explain why you chose your model and metric.
Ask someone to critique the project—and write down what you would change.

phases.title: Make it real
phases.summary: Connect an LLM to code, understand agent loops and MCP, then ship one small, documented tool with safety boundaries.

weeks.title: Call an LLM from code
weeks.focus: Move from chat windows to a small program with inputs, outputs, and secrets handled properly.

tasks.label: Work through the first half of AI Python for Beginners.
tasks.detail: The API examples are optional; the point is code confidence. Use a free-tier or local model if you prefer.

tasks.label: Build a tiny CLI that takes text and returns a labeled summary.
tasks.detail: Put API keys in environment variables. Never paste a key into a tracked file, screenshot, or chat.

tasks.label: Add a README with setup, failure cases, and a privacy note.
tasks.detail: Document what happens when the input is empty, the API fails, or the output is nonsense.

weeks.stretch: Try a local model with a small open model runner and compare latency, quality, and privacy.
weeks.outcome: A small AI script you can run, explain, and safely share.

weeks.title: Build an agent loop
weeks.focus: Understand agents as a loop with tools and stopping conditions—not as magic autonomy.

tasks.label: Complete Unit 1 of Hugging Face's Agents Course.
tasks.detail: Take the free fundamentals quiz if you want the certificate. No pressure to do the full challenge yet.

tasks.label: Draw the agent loop: goal, tools, observations, and stop condition.
tasks.detail: Add a failure mode to each box. Where could it loop, use the wrong tool, or trust a bad observation?

tasks.label: Prototype one agent with a safe tool and log every step.
tasks.detail: Use a calculator or a read-only file lookup first. No write actions without explicit confirmation.

weeks.stretch: Use Microsoft's AI Agents for Beginners as a second perspective on patterns and RAG.
weeks.outcome: An agent mental model and a small, legible prototype.

weeks.title: Give the agent a safe tool
weeks.focus: Learn MCP, then design for least privilege before adding capability.

tasks.label: Complete Unit 1 of Hugging Face's MCP Course.
tasks.detail: The free fundamentals quiz is the natural checkpoint.

tasks.label: Read the opening sections of the official MCP docs and write three sentences about servers, clients, and tools.
tasks.detail: Use your own words. Jargon you cannot explain is jargon you cannot debug.

tasks.label: Design a read-only tool and write a safety checklist.
tasks.detail: List its permissions, data source, what it cannot access, when a human must approve, and where secrets live.

weeks.stretch: Follow a Microsoft MCP for Beginners lab or complete the rest of the Hugging Face MCP course.
weeks.outcome: A clear MCP mental model and a safety checklist for tool use.

weeks.title: Ship, document, review
weeks.focus: Finish one small thing properly and decide what comes next.

tasks.label: Scope the capstone in one paragraph: user, problem, demo, and non-goal.
tasks.detail: Small and tested beats ambitious and unfinished. Choose one narrow task.

tasks.label: Build and test from a clean setup.
tasks.detail: Remove personal data and secrets. If a fresh run needs undocumented steps, fix the README or remove the step.

tasks.label: Write the README and share a short case study.
tasks.detail: Include the problem, audience, how it works, privacy, what works, limitations, and one next step.

tasks.label: Do a 90-day review: list three skills you can demonstrate and two next steps.
tasks.detail: No self-grade or productivity shame. Evidence and a direction are enough.

weeks.stretch: Choose one next specialization: evaluation, safety, fine-tuning, local AI, or product craft.
weeks.outcome: Capstone project, documentation, and a clear next direction.

milestone.title: Day 90 checkpoint: you made a thing
milestone.description: The finish line is not a certificate. It is a working artifact, a readable explanation, and a realistic next step.
checks: A tested tool, notebook, or manual with a README anyone can follow.
One prompt library or workflow you actually reuse.
A personal privacy and safety card for AI use.
A short case study that names limitations instead of hiding them.
A decision about the next 90 days—not a vague intention to 'learn more'.

rules: The plan is the spine; the library is the shelf. You do not need to finish every course.
Three short sessions a week count. Missing a week is data, not a moral failure.
Always protect privacy first: no patient information, client records, passwords, API keys, or private financial data in prompts or repositories.
Use AI for drafts, questions, and scaffolding. Keep human judgment for decisions, claims, and anything high-stakes.
When a resource stops helping, stop. Provider loyalty is not a learning outcome.
If you are exhausted, do the ten-minute version. Rest is part of the schedule.

fallback.title: You missed a week
fallback.text: Restart at the current week. Do not restart from Week 1. Skip the stretch task and keep the next checkpoint small.

fallback.title: You only have 15 minutes
fallback.text: Open the next task, set a timer, and do one small piece. Write one sentence in your learning note before you close it.

fallback.title: A course format is not working
fallback.text: Substitute a video or a different route from the library, but keep the week's artifact. The artifact is the real test.

fallback.title: Life is genuinely on fire
fallback.text: Pause the plan. Keep your notes. When you return, resume at the current week and shrink the next checkpoint. Do not punish yourself with a restart.

fallback.title: Perfectionism shows up
fallback.text: Ship the boring first version. A small, documented thing that works teaches more than a beautiful plan that never runs.

projects.title: For authors and small businesses
projects.text: Build a prompt library for book descriptions, FAQ drafts, and email replies—using only public information. Add a human review step and a fact-check checklist.

projects.title: For healthcare workers, education only
projects.text: Practice with fabricated scenarios. Create a study guide or shift-reflection template, never a diagnostic or treatment tool, and never paste real patient information into a consumer AI tool.

projects.title: For local-first tinkerers
projects.text: Compare a hosted model with a small local model on one low-stakes task. Record privacy, cost, speed, and quality trade-offs in a one-page note.

finishLine: One tested artifact with a README and a clear limitation.
One reusable prompt or workflow, stored somewhere you will find it again.
One personal safety and privacy card.
One honest explanation of what a certificate can and cannot prove.
One concrete next step for the following 90 days.
